stem: A 52-year-old farmer was started on oral itraconazole 4 weeks ago for pulmonary histoplasmosis. His cough and weight loss have not improved. He also takes enalapril and hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure, atenolol, and omeprazole for heartburn. He takes all his pills as directed, and fungal susceptibility testing shows no resistance.
oneliner: 52M farmer + histoplasmosis on oral itraconazole 4 wk + no improvement + takes enalapril, HCTZ, atenolol, omeprazole + adherent, no resistance → which drug is the problem?
ask: An interaction with which of his other drugs best explains the treatment failure?

whyNot.A: Beta-blocker; does **not change gut acid** or itraconazole levels
whyNot.B: ACE inhibitor; **no effect** on itraconazole absorption

answer: Omeprazole (less acid → itraconazole capsules poorly absorbed)
why: **Itraconazole capsules need stomach acid** to dissolve. **Omeprazole raises gastric pH**, so too little drug is absorbed.

drug.name: Itraconazole
drug.how: Blocks fungal CYP450 (lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase) → no ergosterol
drug.use: Histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis
drug.watch: Needs acid to absorb; strong CYP3A4 inhibitor; heart failure risk; liver toxicity

stem: A 62-year-old woman is admitted with fever, flank pain and pyelonephritis with gram-negative bacteremia. She receives intravenous antibiotics for 8 days. She then notes ringing in both ears and difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds. Audiometry shows bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Her creatinine is normal.
oneliner: 62F + pyelonephritis with bacteremia + IV antibiotics for 8 d + tinnitus + bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs most likely caused her hearing loss?

whyNot.B: Gives **tendinopathy and QT prolongation**; not ototoxic
whyNot.D: Gives **hyperkalemia, rash, marrow suppression**; not ototoxic

why: **Gram-negative sepsis + days of IV antibiotics + tinnitus + sensorineural loss** = aminoglycoside ototoxicity. **Gentamicin** damages **cochlear hair cells** irreversibly.

drug.name: Gentamicin
drug.how: Binds 30S ribosomal subunit; concentration-dependent bactericidal killing
drug.use: Serious gram-negative infections, endocarditis synergy
drug.watch: Ototoxicity (hair cells), nephrotoxicity (proximal tubule), neuromuscular blockade; risk rises with loop diuretics

stem: A 41-year-old quadriplegic man with a chronic indwelling catheter is treated with gentamicin for 7 days for a urinary tract infection with gram-negative sepsis. His creatinine rises from 0.9 to 2.6 mg/dL. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts and the fractional excretion of sodium is 3%. He has had no hypotension and no contrast exposure.
oneliner: 41M + quadriplegia, catheter UTI + gentamicin 7 d + creatinine 0.9 to 2.6 + muddy brown casts + FENa 3% + no hypotension or contrast → which nephron site is injured?
ask: Which of the following nephron sites is the primary location of this injury?

whyNot.A: **Nephritic or nephrotic** picture with red cell casts or proteinuria; not muddy brown casts
whyNot.C: Site of **loop diuretic** action; not the usual target of aminoglycosides
whyNot.D: Site of **thiazide** action; not the main injury site
whyNot.E: Site of **lithium**-induced ADH resistance; aminoglycosides accumulate earlier in the nephron

answer: Proximal convoluted tubule injury (aminoglycoside acute tubular necrosis)
why: **Aminoglycoside + rising creatinine + muddy brown casts + high FENa** = acute tubular necrosis. The drug is **filtered and taken up by proximal tubule cells**, where it causes **cell necrosis**.

drug.name: Gentamicin
drug.how: Binds 30S ribosomal subunit; accumulates in proximal tubule cells and cochlear hair cells
drug.use: Serious gram-negative infections
drug.watch: Acute tubular necrosis (reversible), ototoxicity (irreversible), neuromuscular blockade; monitor levels

chain: Filtered, taken up by PCT cells

stem: A 16-year-old girl has taken oral tetracycline for acne for 3 weeks. After a day outdoors she develops a painful skin reaction, shown in the photograph. She has no new soaps, perfumes or topical products, no joint pain or fever and no mucosal lesions.
oneliner: 16F + oral tetracycline for acne 3 wk + painful skin reaction after a day outdoors + no new topical products, no joint pain or fever, no mucosal lesions + photograph → which cause?
ask: Which of the following best explains this skin reaction?

whyNot.A: Seen with **hydralazine and procainamide**, with joint pain and antihistone antibodies
whyNot.C: Idiopathic and **not linked to a drug**; itchy papules rather than a burn
whyNot.E: Has **mucosal erosions and fever**; absent here

why: **Tetracycline + sunburn-like reaction limited to sun-exposed skin** = phototoxic drug reaction (not immune mediated). Other culprits: **doxycycline, amiodarone, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, thiazides**. Advise **sunscreen and sun avoidance**.

drug.name: Tetracycline / doxycycline
drug.how: Binds 30S subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment; absorbs UV light causing phototoxicity
drug.use: Acne, rickettsial and chlamydial infections, Lyme disease
drug.watch: Photosensitivity, teeth and bone staining in children, esophagitis, chelation by cations, contraindicated in pregnancy

image.prompt: Photograph of the shoulders and upper arms of a teenage girl showing sharply demarcated, sunburn-like redness with a few blisters on sun-exposed skin, with a clear pale line where a tank-top strap covered the skin.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is given a 7-day oral course for bacterial vaginosis. On the second evening she drinks two glasses of wine with dinner. Within 20 minutes she has facial flushing, a throbbing headache, palpitations, nausea and vomiting. She has no rash, wheezing or lip swelling.
oneliner: 34F + oral course for bacterial vaginosis + wine on day 2 + flushing, throbbing headache, vomiting + no rash or wheeze → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for her reaction?

whyNot.B: **Clindamycin**: also treats BV but causes C. difficile colitis, **no reaction with alcohol**
whyNot.C: **Ketoconazole**: inhibits steroid synthesis and CYP450; not a treatment for BV
whyNot.D: **Tetracycline**: photosensitivity and tooth staining; no alcohol reaction
whyNot.E: **Mebendazole**: an anthelmintic with no role in vaginal infection

why: **Flushing, headache and vomiting minutes after alcohol on an antimicrobial for BV** = disulfiram-like reaction of **metronidazole**. Acetaldehyde dehydrogenase is inhibited, so **acetaldehyde accumulates**.

drug.name: Metronidazole
drug.how: Free radicals damage microbial DNA
drug.use: Bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, Giardia, C. difficile, anaerobes
drug.watch: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, metallic taste, neuropathy

stem: A 22-year-old African American man is given a 3-day course of an oral antibiotic for dysuria and a positive urine dipstick. The next day he has red-brown urine and fatigue. Scleral icterus is noted. Hemoglobin has fallen from 14.8 to 9.6 g/dL, and the smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies after supravital staining. Serum is pink-red.
oneliner: 22M, African American + antibiotic for UTI + next day red-brown urine, jaundice + Hb 14.8 → 9.6 + Heinz and bite cells → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs most likely caused this reaction?

whyNot.A: **Fluoroquinolones**: tendon rupture, QT prolongation; hemolysis is not the pattern
whyNot.C: **Penicillin**: immune-mediated hemolysis, which does not produce Heinz bodies or bite cells
whyNot.D: **Primaquine**: also hemolyzes in G6PD deficiency, but it is an antimalarial, not given for a urinary infection

why: **Hemolysis within a day, Heinz bodies, bite cells in a man of African ancestry** = G6PD deficiency unmasked by an **oxidant drug**. A **sulfonamide** (TMP-SMX) given for a UTI fits.

drug.name: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
drug.how: Sulfonamide blocks dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase
drug.use: UTI, Pneumocystis prophylaxis and treatment, Toxoplasma prophylaxis, Nocardia
drug.watch: Hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, hyperkalemia, megaloblastic anemia, SJS, kernicterus in neonates

stem: A 25-year-old healthy man has had 2 days of watery diarrhea and cramps after eating undercooked eggs. Stool culture grows Salmonella enterica serotype Enteritidis. He is afebrile and drinking well, and his symptoms are already improving. His physician starts ciprofloxacin anyway. He is seen again 4 weeks later, asymptomatic.
oneliner: 25M, healthy + undercooked eggs + self-limited watery diarrhea, Salmonella + given ciprofloxacin anyway → what is the consequence at 4 weeks?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely consequence of giving the antibiotic?

options.B: Prolonged fecal shedding of the organism

whyNot.A: **HUS**: complicates Shiga-toxin E. coli; no bloody diarrhea, anemia or renal failure here
whyNot.C: **Endocarditis**: no valve disease, fever or murmur is described
whyNot.D: **Anaphylaxis**: would appear within minutes of dosing; he is well 4 weeks later
whyNot.E: **Liver failure**: no jaundice, coagulopathy or enzyme rise is described

answer: Prolonged fecal shedding (carrier state) of Salmonella
why: **Self-limited nontyphoidal Salmonella enteritis in a healthy adult** needs fluids, not antibiotics. Treatment **does not shorten illness** and **prolongs fecal excretion** of the organism.

drug.name: Antibiotics for nontyphoidal Salmonella enteritis (e.g. fluoroquinolone)
drug.how: Kill susceptible organisms, but gut flora disruption lets Salmonella persist
drug.use: Reserve for infants, elderly, immunocompromised, sickle cell, bacteremia or severe illness
drug.watch: Prolonged carriage in healthy hosts with mild enteritis

stem: A 52-year-old man with long-standing alcohol use disorder started a daily oral drug 3 months ago for a positive tuberculin test with a normal chest film. He stopped his multivitamin pills. He now has burning numbness and tingling in both feet in a stocking pattern, with reduced ankle reflexes. Liver enzymes are normal.
oneliner: 52M + alcohol use + 3 mo of latent TB therapy + stopped multivitamin + stocking numbness, tingling in feet → which supplement would have prevented this?
ask: Which of the following would most likely have prevented his symptoms?

whyNot.A: **Folate** deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia; neuropathy is not typical
whyNot.E: **Cobalamin** deficiency: not caused by this drug; it needs dietary or absorption problems

why: **Peripheral neuropathy on latent TB therapy in an alcoholic** = **isoniazid** neuropathy. The drug **depletes pyridoxine (B6)**, so patients at risk get **B6 supplementation**.

drug.name: Isoniazid
drug.how: Blocks mycolic acid synthesis (needs KatG activation)
drug.use: Active TB, latent TB
drug.watch: Hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy (give B6), lupus-like syndrome, CYP inhibition, slow acetylators at higher risk

stem: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with facial pain and a black necrotic lesion on the hard palate. Biopsy shows broad, nonseptate hyphae that branch at right angles. An intravenous antifungal is started. One hour into the first infusion he develops fever of 39.2 C, shaking chills and a blood pressure of 88/52 mm Hg. He has no rash, wheeze or lip swelling.
oneliner: 55M + diabetes + black palatal lesion + broad nonseptate hyphae + IV antifungal started + fever, chills, hypotension during infusion → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs most likely caused this reaction?

whyNot.B: **Fluconazole**: no activity against these molds, and not associated with infusion chills
whyNot.D: **Itraconazole**: oral azole, no infusion reaction; not the drug for these molds
whyNot.E: **Terbinafine**: oral for nails; not used for invasive mold infection

why: **Right-angle branching broad hyphae in DKA-prone diabetes** = mucormycosis, treated with **amphotericin B**. **Fever, rigors and hypotension during infusion** are its classic reaction (**"shake and bake"**); slower infusion and premedication help.

drug.name: Amphotericin B
drug.how: Binds ergosterol, forms membrane pores
drug.use: Mucormycosis, cryptococcal meningitis, severe invasive fungal infections
drug.watch: Infusion fever and chills, nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia

stem: A 44-year-old man with HIV infection has taken a three-drug regimen for 3 years. He has developed a fat pad over the upper back, a wide abdomen, and thin arms and legs. Fasting triglycerides are 480 mg/dL and his glucose tolerance test is abnormal. A 24-hour urinary free cortisol is normal.
oneliner: 44M + HIV on 3-drug therapy for 3 y + upper-back fat pad, wide abdomen, thin limbs + TG 480 + abnormal glucose tolerance + normal cortisol → which drug class?
ask: Which class of drug in his regimen most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.B: **NRTIs**: anemia, pancreatitis, neuropathy, lactic acidosis; not this fat pattern
whyNot.D: **Integrase inhibitors**: weight gain and rash at most; not the lipodystrophy and dyslipidemia picture

why: **Fat redistribution (buffalo hump, central fat, thin limbs), hypertriglyceridemia and impaired glucose tolerance with normal cortisol** = lipodystrophy of **protease inhibitors**, with insulin resistance.

drug.name: HIV protease inhibitors (-navirs)
drug.how: Block Gag-Pol cleavage, leaving immature noninfectious virions
drug.use: HIV, in combination therapy
drug.watch: Lipodystrophy, hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia, CYP3A4 inhibition (ritonavir), GI upset

stem: A 27-year-old nurse is started on zidovudine, lamivudine and lopinavir-ritonavir after a needlestick exposure to an HIV-positive patient. Four weeks later she has fatigue and pallor. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL with MCV of 112 fL, and her absolute neutrophil count is 900/µL. Platelets and liver enzymes are normal.
oneliner: 27F + HIV postexposure regimen of 3 drugs + 4 wk fatigue, pallor + Hb 8.9, MCV 112, ANC 900 → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs in her regimen most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.B: **Protease inhibitors**: lipid and glucose changes, GI upset
whyNot.C: **Ritonavir**: a CYP3A4 inhibitor used as booster; not marrow toxic
whyNot.D: **Enfuvirtide**: is **not** in her regimen; injection-site reactions

why: **Macrocytic anemia plus neutropenia within weeks of starting postexposure therapy** = **zidovudine** (AZT) marrow toxicity. Other NRTIs such as lamivudine rarely do this.

drug.name: Zidovudine (AZT)
drug.how: Thymidine analog; chain-terminates viral DNA made by reverse transcriptase
drug.use: HIV treatment, postexposure prophylaxis, prevention of vertical transmission
drug.watch: Bone marrow suppression (anemia, neutropenia), macrocytosis, myopathy, lactic acidosis

stem: A 39-year-old woman with HIV infection has taken zidovudine and didanosine for 2 years. She now has nausea, abdominal pain, rapid deep breathing and fatigue. Arterial pH is 7.25, bicarbonate is 12 mEq/L, anion gap is 24, and lactate is 9 mmol/L. AST and ALT are elevated and ultrasound shows a fatty liver. Glucose and ketones are normal.
oneliner: 39F + HIV on zidovudine and didanosine for 2 y + nausea, abdominal pain, deep breathing + pH 7.25, gap 24, lactate 9 + fatty liver → toxicity via which enzyme?
ask: Inhibition of which of the following enzymes best explains this complication?

whyNot.A: **Topoisomerase II** inhibitors: etoposide and fluoroquinolones; not these drugs
whyNot.B: **DHFR**: trimethoprim, methotrexate; megaloblastic effects, not lactic acidosis
whyNot.D: **α-amanitin** target; not affected by nucleoside analogs here
whyNot.E: **Nuclear polymerase**: spared by these nucleoside analogs, which prefer the mitochondrial enzyme

why: **Lactic acidosis with hepatic steatosis on zidovudine and didanosine** is **NRTI mitochondrial toxicity**. These nucleoside analogs **inhibit polymerase gamma**, impairing oxidative phosphorylation.

drug.name: Zidovudine / didanosine (NRTIs)
drug.how: Chain-terminate viral DNA; also inhibit mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma
drug.use: HIV, in combination therapy
drug.watch: Lactic acidosis, hepatic steatosis, pancreatitis (didanosine), neuropathy, marrow suppression (zidovudine)

stem: After a smallpox case is confirmed abroad, a hospital offers live vaccinia vaccine to unexposed volunteers for its response team. A nurse screens each volunteer for conditions that make the live vaccine dangerous.
oneliner: Unexposed hospital volunteers + live vaccinia vaccine before any smallpox exposure + nurse screening → which volunteer must not receive it?
ask: Which volunteer should NOT receive the vaccine?

options.D: A person over 65 years of age

whyNot.A: Not an exclusion: the hazard is **replication of live virus** in skin or a weak host, not egg protein
whyNot.B: No link: the hazard is **live virus replication**, not penicillin
whyNot.C: Prior **BCG** gives no interference and no added risk
whyNot.D: Age alone is **not** an exclusion; skin disease and immune status are

answer: A person with atopic dermatitis (eczema vaccinatum risk)
why: The vaccine is **live vaccinia**, which replicates at the site and can spread across **damaged skin**. **Atopic dermatitis** risks **eczema vaccinatum**; **T-cell immunosuppression** risks progressive vaccinia. (After a true high-risk exposure these exclusions are relaxed.)

idea.rule: Live vaccines are dangerous in weak hosts: T-cell defects, severe immunosuppression and pregnancy.
also: MMR, varicella, yellow fever and oral polio are live
Live vaccines are avoided in severe combined immunodeficiency
Pregnancy is a contraindication to live vaccines
Vaccinia is unusual: household contacts with eczema or immunosuppression are also a reason not to vaccinate

drug.name: Live vaccinia (smallpox) vaccine
drug.how: Live vaccinia virus induces cross-protective immunity against smallpox
drug.use: Smallpox and mpox preparedness in selected staff
drug.watch: Eczema vaccinatum in people with atopic dermatitis; avoid in immunosuppression and pregnancy

stem: A 58-year-old diabetic man in ketoacidosis develops facial swelling and black nasal eschar, and biopsy shows broad nonseptate hyphae with right-angle branching. He is started on IV amphotericin B deoxycholate because the liposomal form is unavailable. His ketoacidosis resolves by day 2. On day 10 his creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 2.4 mg/dL.
oneliner: 58M + DKA, resolved + rhinocerebral mucormycosis + amphotericin B deoxycholate day 10 + creatinine 1.0 → 2.4 → which lab finding?
ask: Which additional laboratory finding is most likely?

whyNot.A: Amphotericin damages the **distal tubule**, which **wastes** potassium and magnesium rather than retaining them
whyNot.B: **Hypercalcemia with low phosphate** is a hyperparathyroid pattern, not an amphotericin effect
whyNot.D: **Low sodium with high potassium** suggests adrenal insufficiency; amphotericin lowers potassium
whyNot.E: **High urate and potassium** suggest tumor lysis, which nothing in the stem suggests; amphotericin lowers potassium

why: **Amphotericin B** damages the distal tubule and causes **azotemia with renal wasting of potassium and magnesium** (and a distal renal tubular acidosis). Check **K and Mg** and give saline before doses. **Liposomal** forms are less nephrotoxic and are preferred for mucormycosis.

idea.rule: Amphotericin B toxicity = fever and chills on infusion, then kidney damage with low K and Mg.
also: Infusion reactions with fever and chills (premedicate)

drug.name: Amphotericin B
drug.how: Binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores that leak ions
drug.use: Mucormycosis, cryptococcal meningitis, severe invasive fungal infections
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity (K and Mg wasting), infusion reactions, anemia, phlebitis

stem: A 40-year-old man starts a new HIV regimen of two nucleoside analogs plus an integrase inhibitor. On day 10 he develops fever, diffuse rash, nausea and malaise with a mild cough. He had no genetic testing before starting. Stored blood is later found to carry HLA-B*5701.
oneliner: 40M + new HIV regimen + fever, rash, GI upset, cough at day 10 + HLA-B*5701 positive → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused this reaction?

whyNot.A: Causes **anemia and neutropenia**; it has no **HLA-B*5701** link
whyNot.C: Causes **renal tubular injury and bone loss**, not an HLA-linked hypersensitivity
whyNot.D: Usually well tolerated; it has no link to **HLA-B*5701**
whyNot.E: Usually well tolerated, with **skin hyperpigmentation** the main oddity; no HLA-linked reaction

why: **Abacavir** hypersensitivity is tied to **HLA-B*5701**: fever, rash and GI or respiratory symptoms within weeks. Patients are **screened for HLA-B*5701 before starting**, and rechallenge after a reaction can be fatal.

drug.name: Abacavir
drug.how: Phosphorylated to a guanosine analog that terminates the proviral DNA chain
drug.use: HIV infection, as part of combination therapy
drug.watch: HLA-B*5701 hypersensitivity (screen first; never rechallenge), possible cardiovascular risk, lactic acidosis

idea.rule: Genotype screening before a drug prevents a predictable severe reaction.
also: Carbamazepine with HLA-B*1502 (Stevens-Johnson syndrome in Asian ancestry)
Warfarin dosing with CYP2C9 and VKORC1

stem: A 35-year-old woman has been on an older HIV regimen for several years. She now has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting. Serum lipase is 9 times the upper limit of normal. She drinks no alcohol, her triglycerides are normal, and ultrasound shows no gallstones.
oneliner: 35F + older HIV regimen + epigastric pain to back + lipase x9 + no alcohol, normal TG, no gallstones → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused this complication?

whyNot.A: Causes **marrow suppression and myopathy**, not pancreatitis
whyNot.B: Causes a **hypersensitivity syndrome** with fever and rash
whyNot.D: Causes **renal tubular injury** and loss of bone density
whyNot.E: Usually well tolerated; **pancreatitis** is not its signature toxicity

why: **Didanosine** is the nucleoside analog classically linked to **acute pancreatitis**, along with peripheral neuropathy and lactic acidosis. With **alcohol, triglycerides and gallstones** excluded, the drug is the likely cause.

drug.name: Didanosine (ddI)
drug.how: Converted to a dideoxyadenosine analog that terminates the proviral DNA chain
drug.use: HIV infection (older regimens, rarely used now)
drug.watch: Pancreatitis, peripheral neuropathy, lactic acidosis with hepatic steatosis

idea.rule: Each NRTI has a signature toxicity.
also: Tenofovir: kidney injury and bone loss

stem: A 50-year-old woman has taken combination HIV therapy for 18 months. She has gained fat around the neck and abdomen with a dorsocervical fat pad, while her arms and legs have thinned. Fasting glucose is 168 mg/dL and triglycerides are 480 mg/dL. A 24-hour urinary cortisol is normal.
oneliner: 50F + 18 months HIV therapy + central fat gain + dorsocervical fat pad + thin limbs + glucose 168, TG 480 + normal cortisol → which class?
ask: Which drug class most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.A: Linked to **marrow suppression, neuropathy and lactic acidosis**, not marked **hyperglycemia and hypertriglyceridemia**
whyNot.B: Linked to modest weight gain, insomnia and headache, not marked **hyperglycemia and hypertriglyceridemia**
whyNot.C: Linked to **hepatotoxicity**; it does not raise **glucose or triglycerides**
whyNot.E: Causes injection-site reactions; it does not raise **glucose or triglycerides**

why: **Protease inhibitors** (nelfinavir, ritonavir and others) cause **hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia and lipodystrophy** with **central fat accumulation**, mimicking Cushing syndrome, but **cortisol is normal**. They also inhibit CYP3A4.

drug.name: Nelfinavir (protease inhibitors)
drug.how: Blocks cleavage of the gag-pol polyprotein so immature, noninfectious virions form
drug.use: HIV infection, as part of combination therapy
drug.watch: Hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, lipodystrophy, CYP3A4 interactions (ritonavir boosting), diarrhea

idea.rule: Protease inhibitors cause metabolic syndrome features and CYP3A4 interactions.
also: Ritonavir is the strongest CYP3A4 inhibitor, used to boost other drugs

stem: A 30-year-old man starts once-daily three-drug therapy for newly diagnosed HIV infection. During the first two weeks he has vivid nightmares, dizziness and difficulty sleeping. He has no fever, rash, jaundice or change in blood counts.
oneliner: 30M + new three-drug HIV therapy + vivid nightmares + dizziness + insomnia in first 2 weeks + no rash or fever → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused these symptoms?

whyNot.A: Causes **anemia and neutropenia**; his blood counts are unchanged and it does not cause vivid dreams
whyNot.B: An **integrase inhibitor** that may cause mild headache or insomnia, but not prominent **vivid nightmares and dizziness**
whyNot.C: A **protease inhibitor** causing GI upset and lipid changes, not **vivid nightmares**
whyNot.D: Causes **kidney and bone toxicity**, not **vivid nightmares and dizziness**

why: **Efavirenz** is the **NNRTI** with prominent **neuropsychiatric effects**: vivid dreams, dizziness and insomnia, usually settling in weeks. NNRTIs as a class also cause **rash and hepatotoxicity**, and efavirenz is **teratogenic** in early pregnancy.

drug.name: Efavirenz
drug.how: Binds a hydrophobic site beside the active site of reverse transcriptase and inhibits it allosterically
drug.use: HIV infection, as part of combination therapy
drug.watch: Vivid dreams, dizziness, insomnia, rash, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity, CYP450 induction

idea.rule: NNRTIs share rash and hepatotoxicity, with CNS effects especially from efavirenz.
also: NNRTIs bind reverse transcriptase directly and need no phosphorylation

stem: A 56-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is taking a 9-month course of a single antituberculosis drug plus vitamin B6 for a positive tuberculin test and normal chest x-ray. After 3 months he has nausea, dark urine and jaundice. AST is 1,150 U/L and ALT is 1,320 U/L.
oneliner: 56M + alcohol use + 9-month single-drug latent TB therapy with B6 + nausea, dark urine, jaundice + AST 1,150, ALT 1,320 → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused his liver injury?

whyNot.A: Is used in **4-month or 3-month regimens** for latent TB, not the 9-month single drug he takes
whyNot.B: Causes **optic neuritis** (red-green color loss), not hepatitis
whyNot.C: Used only in **active TB** combinations, not in a latent TB course
whyNot.D: Is the **vitamin B6** he takes to prevent neuropathy and is not hepatotoxic

why: **Isoniazid** causes **hepatitis** that can be severe, more often with **older age, alcohol use and slow acetylator status**. Its liver injury is monitored with transaminases, and **pyridoxine** is given to prevent neuropathy.

drug.name: Isoniazid (INH)
drug.how: Prodrug activated by catalase-peroxidase (KatG) that blocks mycolic acid synthesis
drug.use: Latent and active tuberculosis
drug.watch: Hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine), drug-induced lupus, sideroblastic anemia; slow acetylators at higher risk

idea.rule: Antituberculosis drugs have signature toxicities; isoniazid is the hepatitis and neuropathy drug.
also: Rifampin: orange body fluids and CYP450 induction
Isoniazid hepatitis risk rises with slow acetylators

stem: A 73-year-old man is treated for gram-negative sepsis with a once-daily intravenous antibiotic whose dose is adjusted by drug levels. On day 7 his creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL, with muddy brown casts in the urine, and he reports ringing in the ears and trouble hearing. His trough level is 3.1 µg/mL (toxic above 2).
oneliner: 73M + gram-negative sepsis + once-daily antibiotic dosed by levels + trough 3.1 + creatinine 1.1 → 2.4 + muddy brown casts + tinnitus, hearing loss → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.A: Nephrotoxic too, but its target troughs are **10-20 µg/mL**, so a **toxic level above 2** does not fit, and ototoxicity is rare
whyNot.B: A cephalosporin; not dosed by levels, and it does not cause **tubular necrosis with hearing loss**
whyNot.D: A penicillin; not dosed by levels, and it causes **interstitial nephritis**, not ototoxicity
whyNot.E: A macrolide; not dosed by levels, and it causes **QT prolongation and GI upset**, not nephrotoxicity

why: **Aminoglycosides** cause **acute tubular necrosis (muddy brown casts)** and **ototoxicity**. A **high trough** predicts both, so the dose is guided by **peak and trough** levels and given once daily.

drug.name: Gentamicin
drug.how: Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking the initiation complex and causing mRNA misreading; bactericidal, concentration-dependent
drug.use: Serious gram-negative infections, synergy with penicillins for enterococci and endocarditis
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuromuscular blockade; irreversible hearing loss; avoid with loop diuretics

idea.rule: Aminoglycosides: nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, predicted by a high trough.
also: Ineffective against anaerobes (need oxygen for uptake)
Neuromuscular blockade can worsen myasthenia gravis
